about.title: San Pablo Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: San Pablo's mix of warehouses, retail corridors along San Pablo Avenue and 23rd Street, and industrial sites near I-80 means workplace injuries here range from forklift accidents to repetitive strain from long shifts. Under California law, workers' compensation is generally your only path against your own employer, no matter who was at fault. But when a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver on the job contributed to your injury, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside your comp benefits. Contra Costa County workers often aren't told about this second option. LawProactive doesn't practice law or charge fees; we simply connect injured workers in San Pablo with an independent attorney who reviews the facts and explains what claims might apply. There's no upfront cost, and the attorneys in this network work on contingency, meaning payment only comes if you recover.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney First

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: California generally makes workers' comp the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can still owe you separately. An attorney can spot when a second claim exists.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Move Fast
items.desc: You typically have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and missing that window can complicate your comp claim. Getting guidance early helps protect your rights on both fronts.

items.title: Retaliation Protections Exist
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report injuries or file claims. An attorney can help you understand these protections if you're worried about your job.

items.question: I was hurt at a warehouse job near I-80 in San Pablo. Do I file workers' comp or a lawsuit?
items.answer: In most cases, you'd start with a workers' compensation claim against your employer, since that's usually the exclusive remedy regardless of fault. But if a subcontractor, delivery driver, or faulty equipment played a role, a separate third-party claim may also be available. An independent attorney can look at the specific facts and explain your options.

items.question: How long do I have to act after a workplace injury in San Pablo?
items.answer: You generally need to report the injury to your employer within 30 days to preserve your workers' comp rights. If a third-party claim applies, that typically carries a 2-year deadline under California law. Waiting too long can limit what options remain available to you.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: No, California law prohibits retaliation against employees for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim. If you believe you've faced retaliation, an attorney connected through LawProactive can review the situation and explain your rights.
